title: Nubbin and the Not-So-Neat Plan
markdown:
Now, you see, the Whispering Peaks were a topsy-turvy land of sharp summits and soft cloud-meadows. Ferry ropes, like long, creaky sighs, stretched between them, bridging dizzying chasms. Here lived witch Tilda, who brewed starlight into tea and darned thunderclouds with needle and thread. Her best friend? Nubbin, a hedgehog whose prickles held more good sense than most folk’s entire heads. Usually.

And wouldn't you know it, one crisp morning, the most peculiar thing happened. Tilda needed to deliver a Potion of Perfect Pondering to Mayor Grumbles on the next peak before sundown. This was no ordinary brew; it was for the annual Whispering Peaks Debate, a time for the most serious of discussions.

“Come along, Nubbin, my dear!” Tilda called, her voice as soft as moss. “The sun’s already halfway up the sky! Mayor Grumbles will be pondering without his potion!”

Nubbin, usually as punctual as a mountain sunrise, was nowhere to be found. Tilda searched high and low, peeking under toadstools and behind whispering ferns. She found him, not napping or grub-hunting, but wedged firmly, stubbornly, immovably, in the entrance to his favourite den. His little paws splayed out, his nose tucked in tight. This den feels safe, he thought, but what if the world outside is too loud?

“Oh, Nubbin,” Tilda sighed, her spectacles glinting. “Not now. We cannot possibly be heroically stubborn at precisely the wrong moment! The entire debate depends on this Pondering Potion!”

Nubbin just squeezed his eyes shut, his prickles bristling just a little. No, no, no! This is my safe spot. Everything else is just too… wobbly.

Suddenly, the ground rumbled. Ogre Mallow strode past, his boots like small craters in the soft soil. He had a beard like spun moonlight and a neat, tidy plan for everything. “Tilda, my dear!” Mallow boomed, his voice like friendly thunder. “Trouble with the little spiky one?” He pointed to Nubbin, stuck tighter than a pebble in a plum. “The best way to move a stubborn creature is with a series of precisely placed nudges, followed by a carefully calculated push. Like so!”

Before Mallow could nudge, a gust of wind whipped past, carrying the sharp scent of pine sap and worried chirps of rock-wrens. Tilda noticed the sun dipping lower, casting long shadows. A shiver, not entirely from the wind, ran down her spine. A flutter in her stomach – this is worry, she realised – bubbled up.

Then, a flash of movement. Barnaby Bafflegab, a weasel who could talk the spots off a ladybug, squawked, “Aha! The obvious solution! But the truly clever way is always the most elaborate. You need a contraption! A pulley system!” He pointed to a gnarled oak and a wispy vine. “That’s the neatest-looking plan, surely the cleverest!”

Tilda watched them both. Mallow’s plan was neat. Barnaby’s was elaborate. But Nubbin remained resolutely stuck, a statue of determination.

“My dear child,” Tilda murmured, her fingers tracing her spellbook, “sometimes the neatest plan isn’t the one that gets you where you need to go. It’s the one that listens.” She peered at Nubbin. He wiggled one tiny, determined foot. He’s trying, she thought.

“Perhaps,” Tilda said, as Mallow and Barnaby began arguing about vines versus ogre nudges, “we need a different approach.” She remembered her grandmother’s words: “When all else fails, listen to the stubborn. They often know what the earth knows.”

Tilda knelt beside Nubbin. “What is it, little friend? What are you trying to tell me?” Nubbin gave a tiny huff and pointed his nose towards a small, moss-covered crevice in the rock, usually overlooked.

And wouldn’t you know it, the crevice led to a narrow, winding tunnel. It wasn’t neat, it wasn’t elaborate, but it was different. Tilda, with a gentle coaxing word and a tiny puff of wind magic that tickled Nubbin’s ears, encouraged him forward. He shuffled cautiously, then slid through the crevice, out of Mallow’s nudging range and Barnaby’s ambitious pulley-plan.

“Well, I never!” boomed Mallow. “That was not in my calculations!”
“A mere detour!” sniffed Barnaby, already thinking of a more complex contraption.

But Tilda saw. Nubbin hadn’t been stubborn for no reason. He’d been insistently following his way, a way that felt right to his hedgehog senses.

The tunnel was dark and smelled of damp earth and ancient secrets. Nubbin scurried ahead, his prickles a soft rustle against the earthy walls. Tilda followed, her heart a little lighter, a quiet excitement bubbling within her. “That’s the curious thing about stubbornness,” Tilda whispered, her voice echoing softly. “Sometimes it’s just a different kind of compass, pointing towards a hidden truth.”

They emerged into a hidden grotto, bathed in soft, ethereal light. Sunlight streamed through a crack, illuminating a crystal-clear mountain pool. It was a secret whispered by the mountains themselves.

Barnaby’s elaborate vine contraption was almost there, his triumphant squeak echoing. Mallow, meanwhile, was still diligently calculating the precise angle of his next nudge on a strategically placed boulder.

The path ahead became a narrow ledge, a ribbon of rock clinging to the mountainside. The ferry rope to Mayor Grumbles’ peak swayed precariously in the buffeting wind.

“See!” Barnaby crowed. “My neat, elaborate plan is the fastest! The most reliable!”

But as Barnaby stepped onto the vine, a loose stone tumbled from the cliff face. It struck the vine with a sharp TWANG. The vine snapped! Barnaby yelped, dangling precariously over the chasm.

Mallow immediately abandoned his nudging. “This is highly inefficient!” he declared. “We must secure him! And quickly!” He began devising a plan involving large rocks and a sturdy mushroom.

Tilda watched, her mind racing. The sun was sinking fast. And Nubbin? Nubbin was doing what he did best. He was being utterly, heroically stubborn. He refused to move forward onto the swaying ferry rope. He dug his little paws in, a solid anchor against the howling wind.

“Oh, for goodness sake, Nubbin! We can’t stop now!” Tilda exclaimed, her voice sharper than intended. Then she looked at him. He wasn’t just being difficult. He was looking intently at the ferry rope, then at the crumbling cliff face. He was sensing danger.

“We cannot possibly panic yet,” said Mallow, his booming voice tinged with concern as he surveyed the dangling Barnaby. “We have not even had tea. Efficiency requires proper sustenance.”

Tilda had a sudden, quiet thought. Barnaby’s plan failed because it was too complicated. Mallow’s was too slow. Nubbin was sensing something crucial. His instincts were screaming a warning.

Tilda took a deep breath, calming the anxious flutter in her chest. “Nubbin,” she said softly, abandoning her own plan for crossing the rope. “You’re right. That rope isn’t safe.” She looked at the crumbling cliff face. It was loose and treacherous, but there were tiny handholds, rough patches, places where determination could find purchase. It was Nubbin’s way.

And this is where Tilda truly understood. She trusted her little friend. She was practical, but Nubbin, with his unwavering stubbornness, was her true compass. His intuition was as valuable as any spell.

“Alright, my brave little one,” she said, her voice filled with resolve. She carefully loosened the Potion of Perfect Pondering. Then, with a gentle whisper, she sprinkled a tiny, shimmering drop onto Nubbin’s prickles. It wasn’t to change him, but to help his sensible stubbornness shine even brighter.

Nubbin, with a determined wiggle, began to scramble up the crumbling cliff face. The wind shrieked past, a cold, biting whip against her cheeks. Rough grit scraped her palms, and the dizzying scent of ancient rock filled her lungs. He didn’t sprint; he moved with careful, deliberate steps, his prickles finding tiny crevices, his little paws scrabbling for purchase. Tilda followed, her own hands finding purchase on the rough rock. It was hard work, but Nubbin led the way, a tiny, determined pioneer.

They reached the top just as Barnaby Bafflegab was being awkwardly lowered by Mallow, who had wisely decided a cup of strong mountain tea might indeed be the most efficient next step.

The ferry rope still swayed, a wild, unruly pendulum. But now, Tilda saw it differently. It was a challenge, yes, but not an impossibility. And Nubbin, always the steady one when it mattered most, nudged her forward. He was no longer being stubbornly stuck; he was being stubbornly brave, guiding them towards safety.

Together, they crossed the swaying rope, their hearts thumping a steady rhythm against the wind, landing with a relieved thump on Mayor Grumbles’ peak just as the last rays of sun vanished. The debate was saved. The Potion of Perfect Pondering had arrived just in time.

Tilda hugged Nubbin, careful of his prickles, feeling the solid warmth of him against her. “You see, my dear,” she said, her voice full of quiet wonder, “your stubbornness isn’t a flaw at all. It’s your strength. You always know the right way, even when it’s the hardest way.”

And Nubbin, nestled against her, gave a contented little huff. He had, after all, insisted on his way, and that was the way that mattered.
characters: witch Tilda, hedgehog Nubbin, ogre Mallow
audience: children aged 9-10, amusing mountain adventure fantasy for ages 9-10
